records.text: Why did Network School choose Kazakhstan over 10+ countries? A new conversation with Balaji Srinivasan has just premiered across Trusted Kazakhstan, Astana Hub, and Network State Podcast. Network School is building a global community for people who want to learn tech, work remotely, build companies, and live alongside other ambitious people. Kazakhstan is set to become one of the first major global hubs for this model. In the conversation, Balaji Srinivasan, founder of Network School and former CTO of Coinbase, joins Rinata Ilyubayeva , Managing Director at Astana Hub, and host Thorsten Gutmann to discuss why Kazakhstan stood out among more than 10 countries considered for Network School’s expansion. The discussion goes beyond the decision itself. It explores: • why Astana can become a destination for global tech talent • how digital nomads can contribute to Kazakhstan’s innovation ecosystem • new approaches to education and lifelong learning • how global and local talent can build companies together • Kazakhstan’s growing focus on AI, emerging technologies, and new industries • what the cities and communities of the future could look like One of the central ideas of the conversation is simple: Kazakhstan has the opportunity not only to attract global talent, but to create an environment where people can build, scale, and take tech to international markets. For us at Astana Hub, this is also part of a broader ambition: to make Kazakhstan a place where international founders, engineers, creators, and investors can connect with local talent and build globally competitive tech businesses. Watch the full conversation: https://lnkd.in/eCDdXhGU Join Network School: https://ns.com/ Join the opening of Network School in Astana on September 2: https://luma.com/nskz Meet the global tech community at AI & Digital Bridge, October 1-3 in Astana: https://lnkd.in/d8j2HPmf

records.text: The opening of Saildrone’s EU headquarters in Copenhagen represents much more than a new office. It is part of a long-term commitment to build the people, operations, partnerships, and industrial capacity needed to support autonomous maritime operations across Europe. At Quintus Bastion, we were honored to mark that next chapter alongside Defence Industry Attaché, His Royal Highness Brigadier General Prince Joachim of Denmark; The Honorable Dale R. Marks; Erik Balck Sørensen of EIFO ; Saildrone Founder and CEO Richard Jenkins; our European Managing Director Robert Kleist ; and customers, partners, and members of the Saildrone team. As the speakers reflected throughout the day, building sovereign European capability does not mean working in isolation. It means bringing together European manufacturing and technology, strong transatlantic relationships, public and private investment, and proven autonomous systems to strengthen maritime security and resilience. Our ambition is clear: to build the European capability to manufacture, deploy, operate, and support Saildrone USVs from the region, for the region.

records.text: Lt. Gen. Joseph Jarrard, deputy commander of NORTHCOM, said this month: "We don't have the sensors... We are ill-equipped right now to handle something like that... We're seeing it used on a daily basis around the world, and we've got to figure out how to mitigate that threat. But we're not there yet." He also separately said: "Detection is obviously the biggest issue, and so how we are able to detect is one of our biggest concerns right now." Meanwhile, the counter-drone vendor pitch for 2026 is almost uniformly "layered defense" — stack an RF detector, an AI-video classifier, a kinetic or non-kinetic effector, and call it depth. Several recent product launches lead with AI video fused to RF as the differentiator. Here's the disconnect. A three-star just told the public the bottleneck is sensors and detection, not effector diversity. And detection at swarm tempo isn't really a sensor-count problem — it's a track-correlation problem. Every additional modality is another stream that has to be time-aligned, classified, and reconciled with the others before anyone can act. Add a sensor without solving fusion latency and false-positive suppression, and you've made the decision harder, not easier, against a swarm that's inside your OODA loop in single-digit seconds. If you're building in this space, the question worth obsessing over isn't "what's my next sensor modality." It's "how fast and how reliably does my fusion engine resolve conflicting tracks into one actionable picture" — because that's the gap NORTHCOM's own leadership is naming publicly, not a gap in sensor variety. Where do you think the real bottleneck is — sensor coverage, fusion latency, or engagement authority? #DoW #Defense #Autonomy #CUAS

records.title: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: The new National Security Science & Technology Strategy names undersea, space, and AI/autonomous systems as its top three priorities. Read quickly, that looks like a flat list of
records.text: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: The new National Security Science & Technology Strategy names undersea, space, and AI/autonomous systems as its top three priorities. Read quickly, that looks like a flat list of three coequal domains. It isn't. Undersea and space are physical domains. AI and autonomous systems are a technology category. Pairing them isn't redundant; it's the strategy explicitly stating which capability dictates our ability to operate in those specific environments. Both domains share a critical constraint: you cannot assume a reliable link back to a human. A UUV can't surface for a GPS fix, or burst-transmit a position report, without giving away exactly where it is. A satellite, light-seconds from ground control, cannot wait for a human in the loop to execute a dynamic defensive maneuver. In both cases, AI isn't a third priority alongside them — it's the fundamental precondition for the other two working at all. This points to a concrete positioning strategy. If your technical bet is a decision architecture built to operate without a link home — how it resolves conflicting sensor input, operates under uncertainty, and decides when to hold versus act — that architecture doesn't care whether the external physics involve water pressure or orbital mechanics. It's the same class of problem wearing two different sets of physics. Building and selling that decision layer as portable, domain-agnostic IP is what allows a company to sell into both halves of this strategy's hardest domains, rather than getting boxed into a single platform. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

records.title: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: You can't verify a neural network the way you can verify a PID controller — decades of control theory give you closed-form stability guarantees over the whole operating envelope;
records.text: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: You can't verify a neural network the way you can verify a PID controller — decades of control theory give you closed-form stability guarantees over the whole operating envelope; NN verification tools exist, but they scale poorly and only cover narrow, pre-specified properties over bounded inputs, not the real world your vehicle actually flies through. The pattern (often called Simplex, after Lui Sha's original work at Illinois) is simple to state and hard to build correctly: run your high-performance ML controller as the primary. Run a much simpler, formally verifiable baseline controller in parallel — one that can't do the mission well, but can be proven never to violate the safety envelope. A decision module — the actual hard engineering problem — watches system state and switches to the baseline before the envelope is breached, not after. Get the switching logic wrong and you get two failure modes, both bad: switch too conservatively and your ML controller never gets to do anything interesting; switch too late and the baseline can't recover in time. The switching threshold has to be derived from your vehicle's actual dynamics and worst-case latency, not picked as a round number. This is also why RTA architecture keeps showing up in DoW flight test programs pairing aggressive ML controllers with certified safety systems and automatic recovery — the government isn't asking "is your AI good," it's asking "what happens in the 0.1% case, and can you prove it." If your pitch deck shows an ML controller with no separately-verified safety layer next to it, that's the first thing a government test team asks about — long before they ask about your accuracy numbers. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

The work began after we announced our strategic partnership in October 2025 to combine Saildrone unmanned surface vehicles with Lockheed Martin’s combat-proven effectors. Teams then worked together to integrate the Joint Air-to-Ground Missile (JAGM) launcher onto a Saildrone Surveyor and prepare SD-3001 for the demonstration in Hawaii. Surveyor was already operationally proven. JAGM was already combat-tested. The challenge was to bring the two together quickly and integrate the USV into a Navy fleet environment. SD-3001 is now well on its way to its next mission. The work with Lockheed Martin continues, with this demonstration helping de-risk larger payload integrations planned for Saildrone Spectre. Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: The new National Security Science & Technology Strategy names undersea, space, and AI/autonomous systems as its top three priorities. Read quickly, that looks like a flat list of three coequal domains. It isn't. Undersea and space are physical domains. AI and autonomous systems are a technology category. Pairing them isn't redundant; it's the strategy explicitly stating which capability dictates our ability to operate in those specific environments. Both domains share a critical constraint: you cannot assume a reliable link back to a human. A UUV can't surface for a GPS fix, or burst-transmit a position report, without giving away exactly where it is. A satellite, light-seconds from ground control, cannot wait for a human in the loop to execute a dynamic defensive maneuver. In both cases, AI isn't a third priority alongside them — it's the fundamental precondition for the other two working at all. This points to a concrete positioning strategy. If your technical bet is a decision architecture built to operate without a link home — how it resolves conflicting sensor input, operates under uncertainty, and decides when to hold versus act — that architecture doesn't care whether the external physics involve water pressure or orbital mechanics. It's the same class of problem wearing two different sets of physics. Building and selling that decision layer as portable, domain-agnostic IP is what allows a company to sell into both halves of this strategy's hardest domains, rather than getting boxed into a single platform. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: You can't verify a neural network the way you can verify a PID controller — decades of control theory give you closed-form stability guarantees over the whole operating envelope;

Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: You can't verify a neural network the way you can verify a PID controller — decades of control theory give you closed-form stability guarantees over the whole operating envelope; NN verification tools exist, but they scale poorly and only cover narrow, pre-specified properties over bounded inputs, not the real world your vehicle actually flies through. The pattern (often called Simplex, after Lui Sha's original work at Illinois) is simple to state and hard to build correctly: run your high-performance ML controller as the primary. Run a much simpler, formally verifiable baseline controller in parallel — one that can't do the mission well, but can be proven never to violate the safety envelope. A decision module — the actual hard engineering problem — watches system state and switches to the baseline before the envelope is breached, not after. Get the switching logic wrong and you get two failure modes, both bad: switch too conservatively and your ML controller never gets to do anything interesting; switch too late and the baseline can't recover in time. The switching threshold has to be derived from your vehicle's actual dynamics and worst-case latency, not picked as a round number. This is also why RTA architecture keeps showing up in DoW flight test programs pairing aggressive ML controllers with certified safety systems and automatic recovery — the government isn't asking "is your AI good," it's asking "what happens in the 0.1% case, and can you prove it." If your pitch deck shows an ML controller with no separately-verified safety layer next to it, that's the first thing a government test team asks about — long before they ask about your accuracy numbers. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy
